title: Sea otters, sea urchins and kelp forests: biology, fur trade history and recovery

sources.title: Sea Otters Are Unlikely Helpers in Our Fight Against Climate Change (September 2022)
Sea Otters (Southeast Alaska Inventory and Monitoring Network)

sources.publisher: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries
sources.title: Wildlife Health at Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary

facts.text: Adult sea otters have no blubber and little fat under the skin; they rely on clean, dense, water-resistant fur to stay warm.
Sea otter fur can have up to a million hairs per square inch, compared with about 100,000 hairs on a whole human head (about 10 times as many).
An adult sea otter must eat food equal to 20 to 30 percent of its body weight each day to survive in cold water.
Sea otters eat clams, crabs, sea urchins and snails, and they use rocks as hammers or anvils to open hard shells.
Sea urchins graze on kelp; when sea otters are present in healthy numbers they keep urchin numbers in check, but when otters decline, urchin numbers explode and kelp is damaged.
With fewer urchins grazing, kelp grows and the nearshore ecosystem becomes more diverse.
The sea otter is called a keystone species of the kelp forest ecosystem.
Kelp can grow up to two feet a day.
Sea otters were hunted nearly to extinction for their fur between 1741 and 1911.
Before the fur trade there may have been up to 300,000 sea otters; by the early 1900s only about 13 small remnant groups were left.
A 1911 international treaty banned hunting sea otters in international waters and gave them their first protection.
In the late 1960s, 413 sea otters were moved to several places in Southeast Alaska, and the population there recovered.
Moving sea otters to new places accounts for about 30 percent of the world's sea otters today.
California's southern sea otters number around 3,000 and have returned to only about 13 percent of their historical range, from San Mateo County to Santa Barbara County.
Along the 217 miles of coast between San Francisco and the Oregon border, kelp canopy has fallen by more than 90 percent after a marine heat wave and an overpopulation of purple sea urchins.
